Joining MRA in 2022 as Chief Operating Officer and President, she oversaw growth in research investment and philanthropic and corporate partnerships.

Kauffman will replace Marc Hulbert, Ph.D., who is leaving MRA to become CEO of the National Kidney Foundation. The Board recognized Dr. Hulbert’s contribution to strengthening the position of MRA as a melanoma research funding leader, and notes that he will continue to serve as a member of MRA's Scientific Advisory Panel.

According to Debra Black, Co-Founder and Chair of the Melanoma Research Alliance, in Kauffman’s previous role she “has earned the trust and respect of our Board, staff, researchers, donors, and patient community through her leadership, vision, and unwavering commitment to our mission.” Under Kauffman’s leadership, MRA plans to continue expanding their investments in groundbreaking rare melanoma research and patient centered innovation to improve conditions for patients worldwide.

>Ardent Health President and CEO Marty Bonick "has stepped down to pursue other opportunities," the for-profit health system announced this week. Replacing him immediately is Dave Caspers, who had been serving as chief operating officer.

Bonick helmed the company through a string of challenges, including the COVID-19 pandemic and its 2024 initial public offering. Board Chairman Mark Sotir noted that work in the announcement and said the former head executive had positioned Ardent "for sustained long-term growth and help[ed] build a strong foundation as the Company continues to navigate industry headwinds with a focus on disciplined execution. We wish him all the best in his next chapter."

Caspers, meanwhile, joined Ardent in March 2025 but has spent decades in operational roles. These include senior healthcare leadership positions at Walmart Health, Banner Health and Target. He's spent the past year in the weeds of Ardent's IMPACT (Improve Margins, Performance, Agility and Care Transformation) Program.

"Over the past year, I have had the privilege of working closely with Marty, whose leadership and guidance have been instrumental in laying the solid footing on which Ardent Health now stands," said Caspers, who has also joined Ardent's board. "Today, Ardent Health and our best-in-class team are well-positioned to accelerate our next phase of growth, and I am eager to build on this momentum with a continued focus on delivering high-quality care to the communities we serve.”

>Drew Altman, M.D., founding president and CEO of the influential heath policy research, polling and news nonprofit KFF, will retire from his roles at the end of this year.

He formed the organization in 1990 out of the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation, and has since expanded its scope to include the country's largest newsroom focused on health policy, KFF Health News.

“With two small grandkids in Sacramento and Atlanta and another on the way, after what will be almost 37 years of very hands-on leadership since I founded KFF, and with KFF at the apex of its effectiveness, and the opportunity for a perfect transition, the clock in my head is telling me it’s time,” Altman said in this week's announcement.

Following the recommendation of a search committee, KFF has unanimously appointed two in-house leaders to take on Altman's titles: Larry Levitt, currently executive vice president for health policy, as CEO; and Mollyann Brodie, Ph.D., currently executive vice president and chief operating officer, as president.

The pair have a combined six decades of experience at KFF already under their belt, and will take on board positions with their new roles. They will work with Altman to ensure a smooth transition through the end of the year, officially stepping into his shoes in January 2027

>Visory Health, a prescription savings program, has promoted two executives: Alexandra Robertson to chief growth officer, and Brittney Tierce to chief technology officer.

Robertson started as vice president of growth, driving the company's expansion and presence in more than 38,000 pharmacies nationwide. She will now oversee growth strategy, partnership development and program innovation.

"Visory is positioned to redefine what prescription access looks like for underserved populations, making affordability and access the norm, not the exception," Robertson said in a press release shared in advance with Fierce Healthcare.

Meanwhile, Tierce created the tech underlying Visory. She will now drive the tech strategy company-wide, including security, tech and AI innovation.

"Technology should be a bridge, not a barrier," Tierce said in the announcement. "My focus is raising that bar continuously by creating smarter systems, faster delivery and infrastructure that scales access to the communities we serve."

> Healthcare AI company Abridge brought on board a new chief technology officer, San Oo, as it expands its technology into more health systems. Oo joins Abridge after previously holding leadership roles at Slack and Notion, two popular workplace and productivity software tools.

At Notion, Oo set engineering goals and directions, with a strong focus on reliability, developer velocity and agentic engineering, according to an Abridge press release. At Slack, he helped build the engineering organization during the "hypergrowth years" that defined modern workplace collaboration. Earlier, he served as CTO at ShopBack, a unicorn in the Asia-Pacific region. He was also a founding member of two companies that were later acquired: Mumbo Inc., acquired by LinkedIn in 2012, and Astro Technology, acquired by Slack in 2018.

"The platforms San helped build altered the texture of work with thoughtful technology and exceptional craft that facilitate human connection,” Shiv Rao, M.D., CEO and founder of Abridge, said in a statement. “Healthcare is the next industry that needs that kind of care and platform-level rethink, and San is the rare engineering leader who's done it multiple times."

Abridge is rapidly scaling its AI scribe and clinical decision support technology. It is live in more than 270 of the largest health systems in the U.S., including Duke Health, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Sutter Health and Yale New Haven Health. The platform will support more than 100 million patient conversations in 2026.

"I've spent my career building products and platforms that people love to use that are secure and reliable. Now I want to do the same for healthcare, where the stakes are even higher,” Oo said in a statement. “Abridge already sits at the center of the most important moment in healthcare, the conversation between a clinician and a patient. The opportunity now is to extend that intelligence across the entire system."

> Alignment Healthcare has announced multiple leadership changes that it says will power up the company for long-term growth.

In an announcement, the insurtech said that CEO John Kao has also been named as chairman of the board, allowing him to work more closely with board members. Alongside this shift, previous board chair Joseph Konowiecki has been named vice chairman and as Alignment's executive vice president of corporate affairs.

In the role, Konowiecki will provide critical enterprise-wide leadership as the team looks to build scale, Alignment said in the announcement. Konowiecki is a veteran healthcare executive.

Mark Kent will also join Alignment as president of its management services organization, or MSO. Kent brings experience in value-based care and primary care to the position, having previously held leadership roles in Humana's primary care division, Alignment said.

Alignment Healthcare has also tapped Shane Hochradel as its new chief operating officer. Hochradel has held leadership positions at Elevance Health, Highmark and UnitedHealth Group, per the announcement. All three executives will report to Kao.

“Together, these leadership additions strengthen Alignment’s operating model and position the company well for sustained growth and execution at scale,” Kao said in the announcement.

> Highmark Health has tapped former UnitedHealth Group executive Heather Cianfrocco as its new chief operating officer.

In her time at UHG, Cianfrocco held multiple key leadership positions, including serving as CEO of Optum where she helmed its three core business lines: Optum Rx, Optum Health and Optum Insight. She was most recently the healthcare giant's executive vice president of governance, compliance and information security.

She announced her departure from UnitedHealth in March.

"We have boldly said that we want to be one of the organizations that solves the complex and fragmented health care system," said David Holmberg, Highmark Health CEO, in the announcement. "Heather is a seasoned, innovative health care leader who has a broad national lens, and her skills will be critical as we strive to further expand the reach of our mission and accelerate the work we are doing to transform our industry."

Highmark President Karen Hanlon will continue to lead the company's Living Health initiative, per the announcement.

> Emad Rizk will join Premier, Inc. as its new president and CEO, the company announced.

Rizk, M.D., comes to Premier from healthcare analytics company Cotiviti, where he also served as president and CEO. In the new role, Rizk will be tasked with continuing to drive Premier forward as it seeks to support better patient outcomes at a lower cost.

“I’ve seen healthcare from every angle, and I know what is at stake for Premier’s members,” said Rizk in the announcement. “Providers are being asked to do more with less in an environment that is only getting more complex. Premier has the scale, the data and the relationships to help providers make better decisions and deliver better outcomes. This is where we can make the greatest impact.”

> Alexander Billioux, M.D., is joining the executive team at Cityblock as chief health officer.

Billioux spent the last five years at UnitedHealthcare, where he most recently served as chief medical officer for government programs. He also held leadership roles at the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation and the Louisiana Office of Public Health.

In his new role, Billioux will spearhead Cityblock's clinical strategy and care operations as the company looks to continue advancing its care model.

"I've always been passionate about ensuring that the opportunity for quality healthcare is accessible for all populations. For a large part of my career, that has meant supporting members who face increasing financial and social challenges," Billioux said in the announcement. "Joining Cityblock allows me the opportunity to leverage ground-breaking technology to empower teams to deliver high-quality, comprehensive care that improves the health of vulnerable members."

> Blue Shield of California has named Hayley Park as its new senior vice president and chief pharmacy officer.

In the role, Park will lead the charge on Blue Shield's Pharmacy Care Reimagined initiative, which eschews traditional pharmacy benefit management models for an "unbundled" approach that leans on multiple solutions to offer different elements of the benefit.

Blue Shield said Park brings more than 25 years of experience to the position, and that she served most recently at Kaiser Permanente Northern California as president of pharmacy operations and services.

“What drew me to Blue Shield is that it’s a mission-driven nonprofit health plan that’s committed to improving member health and their lives—not just lowering costs for medications,” Park said. “As pharmacy care shifts to support individuals in a more connected and personalized way, I am excited to join an organization that is transforming healthcare to make it more accessible for everyone.”

Janice Nevin, M.D., will end her 12-year run as president and CEO of ChristianaCare on Sept. 1, the system's board announced.

She retires after 23 years at the organization, initially joining as its chair of family and community medicine. The physician executive is credited by the board with expanding the system's physical footprint, shepherding "significant investment in historically under-resourced areas" and strengthening its academic partnerships.

Taking up the mantle will be Jenn Schwartz, who was named executive vice president and chief strategy officer at the top of 2026. She came to ChristianaCare in 2018 to initially serve as chief legal officer. Prior to that she spent over a decade at Lourdes Health System, where she was vice president of legal affairs & general counsel as well as its executive director.

> Maui Health CEO Lynn Fulton will be stepping down on May 3 after a little over two years in the Hawaiian health system's top role. She plans to return to central Illinois to be closer to her family, according to the announcement that promises a leadership transition plan "in the coming days."

> Samuel Marchio was named senior vice president, chief government relations and policy officer at Ascension, per a social media post. He comes off a 15-year stint at Elevance Health (initially Anthem), where most recently served as regional vice president of federal government affairs.

> Stephen Taluja was named chief mission officer of Providence, a role that tasks him with aligning the Catholic nonprofit system's charity and service aims with ongoing strategic and organizational transformation. The appointment takes effect on June 29.

Nemecek's experience in the payer market will be key to informing this work, according to an announcement.

> Oraida Roman has been named as Aledade's new chief commercial officer, the company revealed on Wednesday. In the role, she will be tasked with leading the team's strategy around national health plan partnerships.

That approach brough national recognitions and designations to its facilities, plus new developments like a genomic program bringing precision medicine into patient care.

Carson, meanwhile, will take on an expanded role in overseeing Centene's Medicare Advantage, Part D, dual-eligible and specialty populations. He joined the company as CEO of WellCare in 2024, and previously held leadership roles at Bright Healthcare and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care.

"Their collective experience will be instrumental as we continue to strengthen performance across the portfolio and deliver sustainable, profitable growth," she said.

The executive stepped into his role in 2014, and was credited by the organization in its announcement release for guiding the system "through some of the most complex public health challenges in modern U.S. history while leading significant transformation across the organization’s clinical, digital and operational capabilities."

The physician executive has been with the organization for four decades, and has sat at its head for the past 12 years. Under his leadership St. Jude underwent the largest strategic expansion in its history, which included the completion of two separate strategic plans requiring nearly $20 billion of investment and over 2,300 new positions; major expansion to St. Jude's main campus; and greater international collaboration.

Prior to that he served as scientific director for eight years, a period in which he spearheaded the Pediatric Cancer Genome Project.

Downing plans to transition into a faculty role at St. Jude's Department of Global Pediatric Medicine after handing over the reins. The organization said a replacement is expected to be named over the summer.

The Post reported that the shakeup comes amid significant controversy over the shift at HHS in vaccine policy and other hot-button topics. Kennedy is looking to shift talking points to more politically palatable topics, like healthy food, per the Post.

“Our exceptional new executive team will be integral to the Federation’s success as we write our next chapter,” MacDonald said in the announcement. “We’re at a critical moment for health care coverage and access, and our team’s proven ability to be strategic, nimble, and relentlessly solutions-oriented will allow the Federation to deliver for our members and the millions of patients they serve.”

He also held key staff roles on the Hill, according to the announcement.

“David Marin is the ideal leader for PCMA at a time of significant change in our industry,” said PCMA Board Chair Adam Kautzner, President of Express Scripts and Evernorth Care Management.

In addition to Marin's hire, PCMA announced that Brendan Buck will serve as the organization's new chief communications officer, also effective on Jan. 20. Buck joins PCMA from public affairs firm Seven Letter.

#5791. 1970 Oldsmobile 442 For Sale With 3,000 Miles Shown Is Ready To Daily With A 455 V8

Among the uninitiated, the Oldsmobile 442 name may not be as recognizable of a muscle car nameplate as the Mustang, Camaro, or Charger, but car enthusiasts know that it's just as muscular a car as the big names. Early '70s 442 models, which came equipped with the 455 cubic-inch or 7.0-liter V8, were especially muscular, which Oldsmobile claimed made 370 horsepower, though that number is commonly believed to be a conservative rating intended to appease insurance companies.

This numbers-matching 1970 Oldsmobile 442 is an unreasonably clean example of its breed, complete with a handful of modernizations that would make it a rather fetching daily driver. It likely won't see daily-driver duty, though, since the miles are so low. It shows just 3,039 miles on its odometer, and it's listed for sale on Hemmings at an asking price of $59,900.

The aforementioned modernizations include a Vintage Air climate control system, a modern stereo hidden in the glove box, and a Tremec five-speed manual transmission, though the iconic original Muncie M-21 four-speed manual is included in the sale, as is an 8-track player.

So long as you can afford to keep it fueled, the odometer should be ignored. This 442 is just begging to be driven – it's been babied for long enough. Its legendary 455 block has been rebuilt and bored with high compression pistons, high-flow heads, a performance intake, and Holley carbs, so it's more than ready to lay down some rubber.

Thanks to that babying, its interior is mostly original. The white seat covers have been replaced along with the carpeting, but its dashboard and door panels are the same ones that were fitted to it from the factory. It's finished in Twilight Blue Metallic with a contrasting white interior and white decals, and the paint only has a few small chips. It's also fitted with an exceptional New York license plate that reads "IV IV II" and is currently located in Bayville, New York. It's priced a bit higher than other 442s, but its ultra-low mileage, fortified engine, and modern touches likely justify its price.

#5790. Hawaii Doctors May Soon Start Prescribing Fresh Food

— The federally funded initiative will start as soon as January

More than 100,000 Hawaii residents who qualify for Medicaid may soon find their doctors prescribing them fresh food as medicine.

The script could be for fresh fruit and vegetables, even ahi, beef, chicken, and eggs. The federally funded initiative will start as soon as January as part of a special state Medicaid program aimed at addressing chronic diet-related health issues in low-income communities.

The Food Is Medicine program could help many in Hawaii, where 1 in 3 households have limited access to safe, affordable, and nutritious food. It could also boost the local agricultural sector, as state advocacy and health groups have tailored the program to promote the use of local produce, which could inject millions of dollars into the economy and create almost 1,000 new jobs.

"It's really a no-brainer," said Alicia Higa, chief health equity officer at Waiʻanae Coast Comprehensive Health Center. "If there's an opportunity to give food as medicine to our people, we should absolutely be using that money to support the local farmers. We'll have an increased food supply, and we'll be much better off.... Not to mention it's the pono thing to do."

Conventional medicine has long turned a blind eye to the importance of nutrition, but its influence on health has been gaining greater attention with the uptick in obesity and diet-related illness globally. In Hawaii, where food insecurity and diet-related diseases are rife, advocates hope the move will help ensure lower income communities have sufficient food and that the food is nutritious and patients are well-versed in healthy eating.

Hawaii has long held goals to address its lack of a local food supply and winnowing population of farmers, but few programs have been able to meaningfully increase the islands' food security as it continues to be plagued by natural disasters.

Now Hawaii will join at least a dozen states in implementing the nutrition scheme, enabled by the Social Security Act's 11-15 waiver program, which allows for experimental and innovative health programs under Medicaid. The state's program will be rolled out in three phases, starting in January with nutritional education programs and prescription food boxes for eligible patients.

The program has been years in the making.

Healthcare providers and advocates recommend at least 15% of all produce and protein comes from local sources, setting it apart from other states. It's not binding, but it's an aspiration, said Jordan Smith of Hawaii Good Food Alliance, which is one of the program's lead agencies in the initiative. And it's still a work in progress.

"It's a lot of work to bring together a broken healthcare system and a broken food system, and asking them to work together," said Smith, the alliance's Food Is Medicine program manager.

Sourcing food from the continent is certainly an easier option, but healthcare providers are resolved to stay as local as possible. Otherwise, the food is mostly "coming across the ocean on a boat, it's not fresh, it's not necessarily culturally relevant," Smith said. "That's why we're exceptionally excited about the 11-15 waiver."

Big Island residents Moses and Suzette Paio have struggled with health issues associated with diet for years, making little progress in the past. What they could afford to eat plays a major role in their diet.

They're not alone, living on an island where 43% of residents report food insecurity. One-third of the state's households report insufficient access to adequate, nutritious, affordable food, according to Hawaii Food Bank's 2025 State of Food Security Report. And about half of Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders are food insecure, suffering the diet-related health ramifications.

Puna, where the Paios live, is classified as a food desert: a location with limited or no access to affordable, fresh, healthy, and nutritious food.

"It's not that I don't want to buy it," Suzette Paio said, "it's just that I can't."

The Paios took part in a pilot program that rolled out under the Medicaid waiver this year. It included access to five months of weekly produce and protein boxes, delivered by the Food Basket, Hawaii's food bank. The boxes included locally caught and harvested proteins, greens, and fruits.

Suzette Paio's average blood sugar has halved, something she has struggled to get under control for more than a decade. Moses Paio lost over 70 pounds.

Local bananas and papayas, "they're my candy," said Suzette Paio, having replaced cheaper sugary treats she used to enjoy.

The Paios have also started gardening, preserving food, and getting more active, taking lessons from other education programs.

"We just thank God for the opportunity that we had," Suzette Paio said, "because you know our health issues have been going on for a while."

Advocates are encouraged by the data they have been collecting during pilot studies, which have run for at least the past year, though there is much more research to do.

The University of Hawaii (UH), for one, is conducting a 5-year study on the program's influence on hypertension at various healthcare centers on the islands. UH assistant professor of nutrition Monica Esquivel, PhD, RDN, who is leading the study, says much more data will come as the program develops, but its premise is proof of a growing recognition of diet's influence on health.

In West Oʻahu, also considered a food desert, nutritionally focused healthcare programs have been operating since 2017, separate from the Medicaid initiative. The positive results kept them going, said Higa, who is also the CEO of ʻElepaio Social Services.

"We built it because we didn't have it," she said. "I think that's traditionally what Waiʻanae does because we're so far from everything."

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Waiʻanae Comprehensive Health Center tracked almost 500 Medicaid patients over 18 months, Higa said, when they received a $60 monthly produce prescription.

Higa's team tracked how much of the money was used, how the recipients' health changed, and how much it cost insurance. It resulted in about $118 in healthcare savings per patient, per month, she said.

Now, with the Med-QUEST program, the initiative has far greater security, Higa said.

Advocates believe the produce prescription will function like Hawaii's Da Bux program, which doubles the spending power of beneficiaries of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program -- formerly known as food stamps -- when purchasing locally produced food.

There were almost 250,000 Da Bux transactions last year, accounting for more than $5.5 million in local produce, making it a triple win by benefiting the economy, the hungry, and local farmers.

Food Is Medicine could do the same, advocates say, given approximately 121,000 residents could be eligible for the program.

The initiatives could unlock $12.3 million in additional annual revenue for Hawaii farmers, according to a national Rockefeller Foundation analysis, the lion's share benefiting small and mid-sized farms. It could also boost the state's GDP by $125.5 million.

The results for farmers have already been seen on Oʻahu, with Waiʻanae Farmers Market vendors scaling up production in response to demand driven by food-based health programs run by Waiʻanae Comprehensive. The same has happened on the Big Island, with egg producers scaling up to meet demand, according to Food Basket CEO Kristen Frost Albrecht.

Micah Richards of Mauka Meats, a local meat provider, says his business and the ranchers he works with have benefited immensely. And he believes the program holds great promise for the entire agriculture sector.

Some hurdles exist, Richards said, including helping farmers and ranchers get food safety certifications so they can take part.

The greatest payoff from the program, he said, has been "having auntie come up to you at the market, tell you they feel better, they're making progress with their doctor, but all they feel they changed was going to the farmers market and having access to the funds for local meat and produce."

The Medicaid program's official rollout in January will start with prescriptions and nutritional education, but will mostly rely on organizations being able to deliver the service to eligible residents.

The second phase will include helping eligible Medicaid users stock their pantries and acquire cooking supplies, as well as phasing in medically tailored meals. The meals, on a national level, could help reduce the need for 2.6 million hospitalizations annually, a net cost savings of $23.7 billion, according to Tufts University.

The program is being coordinated by Med-QUEST, part of the state Department of Human Services, and the Hawaii Good Food Alliance. But the programs' full rollout will depend on individual health centers and food distributors, Med-QUEST Administrator Meredith Nichols said in an email, adding that the state is providing grants to help increase organizations' ability to deliver the programs statewide.

The prescriptions will give eligible recipients $50 per week to buy fresh protein and produce on Oʻahu, while other islands' residents will receive $55 weekly. The food could come in the form of food boxes, like the Paios get, or in vouchers to be used at farmers markets, like Waiʻanae Coast Comprehensive Health Center's patients do.

Advocates anticipate the program will be popular. On the Big Island, Moses Paio expounds the program's virtues openly, giving tips to friends, family, and members of his church. It's changed his life, he said, now that he's lost weight and can be more active.

"My yard pushes me. I see the grass growing," Moses Paio said. "There are times out there, I'm cutting grass, and I'm just crying. You know, I'm just thanking God that I can even just stand there."

#5789. Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging

Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.

The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.

The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.

"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.

Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike

Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.

To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.

Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.

Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..

A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation

Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.

The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.

In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.

Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:

Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells

The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.

The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.

When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.

Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.

These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.

Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:

A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research

Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.

The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.

Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.

The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.

By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.

Materials provided by Mayo Clinic. Original written by Alison Satake. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5788. Amwell bets AI boom will drive demand for its unified care platform

Amwell bets AI boom will drive demand for its unified care platform" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As health plans and employers contend with a growing array of virtual care and AI-enabled tools, Amwell is positioning its digital health platform as the infrastructure layer for AI-enabled care.

Executives at Amwell, formerly known as American Well, touted the company's platform strategy, government contracts and higher-value clinical services as the main drivers of future growth during the company's third-quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Rising healthcare costs are pushing health plans and employers to adopt tech-enabled care solutions, but they are looking for measurable engagement and outcomes from digital health vendors, not just access, according to Ido Schoenberg, M.D., Amwell chairperson and CEO.

The proliferation of point solutions, accelerated by AI, is creating more vendor sprawl and member confusion, Schoenberg told investors and analysts during the call.

There's also a lack of proof with many digital health tools, he noted. "It is hard to see which programs work and harder still to replace one without disrupting members. That sprawl is accelerating. AI has made it faster and cheaper to build a clinical program. Investors have backed hundreds of new digital health companies this year, many of them built on AI. Our customers feel pressure to offer these programs, but each one brings its own cost, its own integration, and its own front door. The opportunity is real. So is the complexity," he said.

More patients are turning to AI for health guidance, but those interactions don’t necessarily lead them to appropriate, covered care, creating the risk of poor clinical decisions and unnecessary costs for health plans, Schoenberg said.

"This is the problem Amwell is determined to solve for our customers. We help them improve clinical and financial outcomes. We do it through activation, getting more of their members into technology-enabled care in place of conventional care that often costs more. We give our customers one platform under their brand with one integration. It provides reliable, scalable rails to bring in a program, exchange data with it, and tests whether it works. The member's experience stays consistent, simple, and engaging. A common data structure proves the outcomes and improves performance over time," he said.

As AI adoption grows, a unified care platform becomes more valuable, Schoenberg asserted.

"We are not selling an AI feature. We are the trusted platform where AI-powered care runs with clinicians in the loop," he said during the Q3 call.

Amwell's customers represent more than 90 million covered lives, and the company also serves 9.6 million beneficiaries of the Military Health System.

Amwell's platform can help drive member engagement and utilization of digital health tools, executives said.

"Most of the health plans we talk to still see engagement in the single digits. We address that with always-on engagement, outreach to members through our customers' own channels within the rules they set. When a customer switches it fully on, members use the platform at more than three times the rate we see when it's off," Schoenberg said.

The platform runs on a common data structure, he noted. "It sends a member into a program with the right information. It collects outcomes back, and it reports value in the customer's own terms, whether that customer is a health plan or an employer that the plan serves. That is how a program proves its return on investment and how it gets better over time," he said.

In response to a question from an analyst, Schoenberg suggested pricing for the solution could evolve from fixed Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) fees toward outcomes-based arrangements in which Amwell shares in the savings it produces for health plans.

Amwell executives view that platform strategy as key to the company's growth.

In Q3, Amwell reported revenue that was slightly above Wall Street's consensus and a narrower adjusted loss than analysts expected. Amwell executives also reiterated confidence in reaching positive operating cash flow and breakeven to positive adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter.

Amwell brought in $49 million in Q3 revenue, according to financial results published Tuesday afternoon. Revenue was down approximately 12.9% year-over-year, but $1 million above the high end of management's guidance range, according to Chief Financial Officer Mark Hirschhorn.

Subscription revenue was $23.9 million, down approximately 22.5% year-over-year and 6.8% sequentially, Hirschhorn said. “The year-over-year decline continues to reflect the previously disclosed churn we've discussed on prior earnings calls,” he added.

Amwell Medical Group (AMG) visit revenue was $23.7 million, up approximately 11.7% year over year, while AMG paid visits totaled approximately 301,000 visits, essentially flat year over year, Hirschhorn said.

Virtual primary care visits were up 41% year over year, continuing that segment's strong growth trajectory. Total platform visits were approximately 760,000 visits, down approximately 30.5% year over year—though Hirschhorn noted the decline is consistent with previously discussed portfolio changes.

The telehealth platform reported a net loss of $11.7 million during the quarter, compared to a loss of $29.3 million for the same period a year ago, Hirschhorn said. Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $3.6 million from a loss of $12.7 million a year earlier.

Amwell executives are bullish on revenue growth from its own clinical services, including virtual primary care and behavioral health.

Executives also highlighted the company's government business as it delivered solid third-quarter financial performance. Amwell announced in September that the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) issued a letter of intent to deploy its platform enterprise-wide.

"I want to be precise about what this is," Schoenberg said. "The letter is not a binding contract. A definitive agreement still has to be negotiated and executed under federal procurement rules, and that work is underway."

Schoenberg noted the letter followed a "comprehensive evaluation."

"It cited scalable video consultations, interoperability, cybersecurity compliance and support for integrated care delivery," he said. "In plain terms, the capabilities the department evaluated are the ones we already run at scale for the military health system, and the department's own scale is considerable."

Amwell executives are optimistic the company will sign a contract with the VA "over the next couple of months," Hirschhorn said, with implementation beginning in 2027, but no definitive agreement exists yet.

Moreover, Schoenberg said the platform is continuing to negotiate a "direct, longer-term contract" with the Defense Health Agency (DHA).

The DHA, which oversees services for the Military Health System, renewed its contract with the telehealth platform in August 2025. In June, it called for sole contracts with Amwell and four other vendors.

DHA discontinued its payment for behavioral health and automated care services with Amwell last year. Schoenberg said the cessation was due to the Department of Defense’s cost-cutting measures—not the department’s satisfaction with the services.

Hirschhorn said that Amwell is raising its full-year revenue guidance to between $204 million to $206 million, up from $195 million to $205 million. The company now expects full-year adjusted EBITDA to be a loss in the range of $6.9 million to $7.9 million, a meaningful improvement from its prior range of a loss of $12 million to $16 million.

Amwell forecasts full-year AMG visits between 1.32 million to 1.37 million visits.

“In summary, during the third quarter, we exceeded our revenue guidance with stronger visit volumes, a stable subscription base, and a leaner cost structure that positions us to finish the year on a strong note,” Hirschhorn said.

#5787. New Trials Back Quickly Approved Drugs for Primary Biliary Cholangitis

— Results show that biochemical normalization is a "feasible goal," researchers say

Treatment with both elafibranor (Iqirvo) and seladelpar (Livdelzi) led to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) normalization in the vast majority of patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) who had elevated ALP levels after an incomplete response or intolerance to first-line therapy, two phase III trials showed.

Results from the ELSPIRE study showed that 85.3% of patients who received elafibranor achieved the primary endpoint of ALP normalization compared with 23.3% receiving placebo (P<0.0001) at week 52, reported Kris V. Kowdley, MD, of Liver Institute Northwest in Seattle.

The IDEAL trial demonstrated that 75.4% of patients treated with seladelpar achieved ALP normalization versus 16.1% of those receiving placebo (P<0.0001) at week 52, reported Cynthia Levy, MD, of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

Results from both trials were presented at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) annual meeting in Denver, and the ELSPIRE study was also published in Hepatology.

Elafibranor is an oral dual peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) agonist that was granted accelerated approval for the treatment of PBC in adults based on results from the ELATIVE trial.

Meanwhile, the oral PPAR-delta agonist seladelpar was granted accelerated approval for the treatment of PBC in adults based on data from the RESPONSE trial.

"The key issue in our understanding of PBC, and where we are in PBC, is that it has become more and more clear that if you look at the best outcomes in patients that have PBC, it is in those that have achieved normal alkaline phosphatase," Kowdley told MedPage Today. "So, for a long time, we knew that alkaline phosphatase was a predictor of long-term outcomes."

The POISE trial defined biochemical response as the achievement of ALP under 1.67 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), with a reduction of at least 15% from baseline, and a normal total bilirubin level.

"Ever since then, all studies have used alkaline phosphatase of 1.67 above the upper limit of normal as the cutoff for predicting worse outcomes," Kowdley noted. "But, what about patients who have an elevated alkaline phosphatase above the upper limit of normal, but less than 1.67 times the upper limit of normal? That intermediate group ... also has an increased risk of adverse liver-related outcomes over the long term."

Thus, the ELSPIRE researchers sought to evaluate elafibranor in patients with PBC and an ALP over 1.00 but under 1.67 times the ULN after an incomplete response or intolerance to first-line therapy with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA).

"And as a proof of concept, [the study shows] you can achieve normalization in a very high proportion of patients if you start them earlier in the stage of the disease," Kowdley said.

ELSPIRE included 92 patients (median age 61 years, 92.4% women) who had a mean baseline ALP of 149.4 to 151.5 U/L. All patients had ALP over the ULN but under 1.67 times the ULN at randomization, and 96.7% had ongoing UDCA treatment for a median duration of around 5 years.

ALP normalization was considered to be less than or equal to the ULN (defined as ≤120 U/L at week 52) without the use of rescue therapy for PBC, and without experiencing a liver-related event or death due to any cause.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to elafibranor or placebo, and stratified into two categories by ALP (>1 to ≤1.33 times the ULN and >1.33 to <1.67 times the ULN).

Greater proportions of patients in both categories achieved the primary endpoint of ALP normalization with elafibranor versus placebo: 80.4% versus 26.1% in patients with ALP >1 to ≤1.33 times the ULN (P<0.0001), and 87.5% versus 14.3% in patients with ALP >1.33 to <1.67 times the ULN (P=0.0017).

Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were observed in 79% of patients treated with elafibranor versus 70% treated with placebo.

Increased weight was reported in 22.6% of patients receiving elafibranor and 6.7% receiving placebo, with five TEAEs of increased weight considered to be related to elafibranor treatment.

Levy and colleagues (including Kowdley) found that higher response rates were observed at all timepoints with seladelpar, with the effect observed as early as a month into treatment, with 52.3% of seladelpar patients achieving ALP normalization at that time point versus 6.5% in the placebo group.

"These results help inform treatment decisions for an understudied population and demonstrate biochemical normalization as a feasible goal," Levy and colleagues concluded.

In IDEAL, 96 patients were randomized 2:1 to receive seladelpar or placebo for 12 months. Mean age was 61 years, 93.8% were women, and mean baseline ALP was 153 U/L.

Patients were considered responders if they achieved a 15% or more decrease in ALP levels from baseline, and if blood levels of the enzyme were ≤1.0 times the ULN.

Serious adverse events were reported in 3.1% of patients in the seladelpar group and 12.9% in the placebo group, with none deemed related to the drug.

#5786. CMS finalizes steeper Medicare physician pay cuts for 2027, moves ahead with RPM vendor restrictions

CMS finalizes steeper Medicare physician pay cuts for 2027, moves ahead with RPM vendor restrictions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services finalized sweeping Medicare payment reforms it says will shift the program from volume-based "sick care" toward prevention, primary care and accountable care.

The 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule includes a roughly 2% reduction in baseline physician payment rates with targeted increases and new payment opportunities for accountable care, primary and chronic care and behavioral health. CMS finalized steeper physician payment cuts than it had proposed in July.

An unpublished PDF version of the 2,468-page final rule can be found here.

In a press release, CMS said it is "prioritizing prevention, strengthening primary care, cracking down on duplicate billing and reinforcing fiscal stewardship across Medicare."

The final rule modernizes physician payment structures to "reward health maintenance and coordinated primary care rather than disjointed, volume-based intervention," CMS said.

"Medicare should reward clinicians for keeping people healthy," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said in a statement. "Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting prevention and primary care at the center of Medicare, closing payment loopholes, and cracking down on waste. This rule directs resources toward coordinated care that puts patients first. We are changing what Medicare pays for to change what our health system delivers."

Under the final rule, CMS will officially sunset the traditional Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) reporting option beginning with the CY 2031 performance period. Clinicians will have through CY 2030 to transition to the MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs), which already cover approximately 98% of clinicians, or Advanced Alternative Payment Models. This reflects two additional years of transition time compared to the proposed rule. The rule also finalizes three new MVPs focused on diabetes, hypertension and hospitalists, and requires clinicians to report at least one specialty-specific "Core Measure" starting in CY 2027.

The final 2027 PFS rule also establishes new 340B reporting requirements. Covered entities will have to report certain Medicare Part D claims involving drugs purchased through the 340B Drug Pricing Program to the Medicare Part D Claims Data 340B Repository beginning with claims with a date of service on or after Jan.1, 2027. The deadline for the first quarterly submission is delayed until Sept. 30, 2027.

For physicians, while the proposed rule includes statutory payment increases, Medicare payment rates face an overall baseline decrease for 2027 due to the expiration of a temporary 2.5% legislative increase from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in 2026.

Under the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA), the CY2027 conversion factors reflect statutory updates of +0.75% for qualifying Alternative Payment Model (APM) participants and +0.25% for non-qualifying participants. The changes to the PFS conversion factors for CY 2027 include these updates as required by statute and an estimated -0.12% adjustment necessary to account for proposed changes in work RVUs for some services, according to CMS in a fact sheet.

For clinicians who don't qualify through an advanced alternative payment model, the conversion factor drops from $33.40 to $32.63, a 2.31% reduction. For qualifying APM participants, the conversion factor drops 1.83% from $33.57 to $32.95. In the draft rule issued in July, CMS projected cuts of 1.68% and 1.19%, respectively.

CMS is also addressing what it sees as overpayment and duplicate reimbursement when multiple services are delivered during the same patient encounter. Under the final rule, when an office visit and minor procedure occur on the same day, CMS will reduce payment by 20% for the lower-cost service, reducing duplication in payment by patients and the Medicare program for clinical work already covered in the procedure’s valuation.

CMS had initially proposed paying the higher-cost service in full and reducing payment for the other service by 50%.

Physician groups were quick to criticize CMS' payment changes in the final rule.

"Notwithstanding modest policy improvements to enhance value-based care through MSSP, MGMA is disappointed by CMS’s decision to finalize several destabilizing policies in the 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule," Anders Gilberg, senior vice president of government affairs at the Medical Group Management Association, said in a statement.

"Conversion factor cuts of 1.83% for qualifying APM participants and 2.31% for all other clinicians further degrade an already fragile payment system and amplify severe financial challenges caused by years of inadequate Medicare reimbursement," Gilberg said.

Compounding this ongoing reimbursement decline, CMS will cut payments by 20% when office visits billed with modifier 25 are performed on the same day as certain procedures, "interfering with physician practices’ ability to offer same-day care," he noted.

MGMA is urging Congress to intervene by immediately fixing cuts to the conversion factor, along with changes to modifier 25. "To prevent annual disruption, Congress should prioritize comprehensive MACRA reform by passing the Patients First Act," Gilberg said.

The agency is overhauling the office/outpatient evaluation and management visit complexity add-on code, HCPCS code G2211. CMS is transitioning HCPCS code G2211 from a flat add-on payment to a modifier that would increase the payment of the associated E/M code by 16%. That would maintain an equal percentage increase across all levels of E/M codes, CMS said.

The agency also finalized a new modifier that would offset the costs incurred by practitioners in accountable care organizations (ACOs) when providing longitudinal care and care coordination. The modifier would only be available for practitioners participating in a Shared Savings Program ACO or participant providers in a Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model ACO and would increase payment of the associated E/M visit by 32%, CMS said.

In the final rule, CMS tightened remote patient monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring requirements, following through on a controversial ban of third-party RPM vendors. However, CMS delayed that restriction for two years.

Beginning in 2027, as CMS outlined in the proposed rule, RTM services can only be furnished to established patients, and providers must provide a separately reportable initiating visit before billing for RPM or RTM services.

Despite intense industry pushback, CMS completed a proposal that will prevent providers from using third-party vendors or contractors for RPM services. For the purposes of billing, RPM services must be performed by clinical staff employed by the practice, according to the PFS rule. But the agency provided a two-year reprieve on that requirement as it goes into effect Jan. 1, 2029, "giving practices that rely on contractors two additional years to adapt," CMS said.

Health tech companies, providers and lawmakers pushed back on the proposal to restrict third-party vendors, urging CMS to reconsider the proposed changes to preserve patients' access to these tech-enabled services. Many rural, small, and independent practices, as well as both urban and rural health systems, rely on specialized clinical and technology partners to make remote monitoring services available to their patients.

CMS finalized changes to the Medicare Shared Savings Program, the nation’s largest value-based payment program, to "accelerate accountable care service delivery, further CMS' goal of aligning spending and value in Original Medicare, and support achieving other related strategic objectives," the agency said in a fact sheet.

The overhaul to the MSSP program aims to make ACO participation more financially attractive, encourage organizations to take on risk, expand beneficiary participation and ease some quality-reporting requirements.

The agency says the changes are projected to grow the program by adding up to 1 million assigned beneficiaries in an average year and produce $5.5 billion in net federal savings over 10 years. CMS also projects the changes will generate an overall increase in shared savings net of losses to ACOs by $1.1 billion over a decade.

The final rule changes the Shared Savings Program’s benchmarking and financial methodology to balance incentives between Level E of the BASIC track and the ENHANCED track. Under the final rule, the shared savings rate for Level E of the BASIC track increases from 50% to 60%, and it reduces the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs participating under the ENHANCED track from 50% to 35%.

The agency is increasing the prior savings adjustment's scaling factor from 50% to 75%, allowing more of an ACO's previous savings to be reflected in future benchmarks.

Under the final rule, CMS will risk-adjust the 5% cap on benchmark increases, potentially allowing ACOs that care for sicker, higher-cost patients to receive larger upward adjustments.

Data shows patients aligned with an ACO are less likely to experience uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension and are more likely to receive recommended preventive care, according to CMS. In performance year 2024, 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned shared savings totaling $4.1 billion, while generating net savings for the Medicare Trust Funds of approximately $2.5 billion compared to projected spending benchmarks.

Under the final 2027 PFS rule, approved ACOs may reduce or eliminate Part B cost-sharing for many items and services for assigned beneficiaries, directly lowering out-of-pocket costs for essential care. That change goes into effect April 1, 2027.

The rule also increases shared savings rates for eligible ACOs, provides novel incentives for first-time participants and sets more predictable spending targets. The rule also simplifies electronic health record reporting requirements, streamlines patient notice mandates and removes outdated administrative hurdles, CMS said.

#5785. Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease

Scientists from the University of Oxford, Newcastle University, and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust have uncovered a previously unexplained cause of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The discovery could change how doctors understand, diagnose, and treat certain forms of the condition.

The findings indicate that IBD is not simply one disease. Instead, it appears to include several biologically distinct conditions that develop through different processes in the body. Identifying these differences could make it possible to provide treatments tailored to the specific cause of each patient's illness.

In a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers examined more than 4,900 people with IBD and identified two important findings. First, some patients produce antibodies that interfere with interleukin-10 (IL-10), an essential protein that helps prevent excessive inflammation. Second, this autoimmune reaction explains how one of the strongest known genetic risk factors for IBD contributes to the disease.

Under normal circumstances, IL-10 acts as a chemical messenger between cells, helping the immune system regulate inflammation. However, certain antibodies can block its activity, effectively disabling one of the body's built-in safeguards against excessive immune responses. Without this protection, inflammation can persist and become difficult to control.

Hidden Antibodies Reveal a Cause of Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, two chronic conditions that affect approximately 500,000 people in the UK and millions more around the world.

Symptoms often first appear during adolescence or early adulthood, and patients may face lifelong medical challenges. Managing the disease can involve repeated hospital visits, medications that suppress immune activity, and sometimes surgery. Although treatments have improved, many people must try several different therapies without achieving lasting relief. This places a substantial burden on patients and creates significant costs for healthcare systems.

The researchers discovered that approximately 3.5% of patients with IBD had elevated levels of antibodies that neutralize IL-10. These antibodies were detected in people with both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, but not in healthy individuals.

Based on the prevalence of IBD in the UK, the researchers estimate that 15,000 to 20,000 patients nationwide could carry these harmful antibodies.

Scientists Solve a 30-Year Genetic Mystery

The investigation also revealed a strong association between the IL-10-blocking antibodies and a genetic variant called HLA-DRB1*01:03.

Scientists at Oxford first connected this genetic variant to a severe form of inflammatory bowel disease 30 years ago. However, the biological process linking the gene to the condition had remained unclear.

The new results help resolve that longstanding mystery. People who carry HLA-DRB1*01:03 are substantially more likely to develop antibodies that interfere with IL-10, providing an explanation for how this genetic risk factor can contribute to severe intestinal inflammation.

Professor Holm Uhlig, a pediatric gastroenterologist and Director of the Centre for Human Genetics at the University of Oxford's Nuffield Department of Medicine, was a senior author of the study.

"We've suspected an important role of interleukin 10 in patients with inflammatory bowel disease for decades. The study now provides clear evidence and contributes the missing link between a well-known genetic variant that had been linked to severe inflammatory bowel disease in the past and the very recently discovered autoimmunity to interleukin 10."

"Understanding what drives the inflammation, provides a clear explanation for disease in this group of people and opens the door to new treatments that target the autoantibodies themselves or cells that produce those autoantibodies."

How Earlier Discoveries Helped Explain Severe IBD

The findings build on more than a decade of research into rare inherited disorders that disrupt the body's ability to control inflammation.

Sophie Hambleton, Professor of Pediatrics and Immunology at Newcastle University, explained that studying these uncommon conditions provided important clues about the mechanisms involved in more widespread forms of IBD.

"This discovery shows how the study of rare, inherited disorders can shed new light on common conditions. The groundwork was laid over 10 years ago when genetic defects in IL-10 or its receptor were found in young children with severe IBD. Later, we realized that neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-10 were mimicking this effect in 2 little girls with colitis."

These earlier observations helped researchers recognize that antibodies blocking IL-10 could produce effects similar to inherited defects involving the same protein or its receptor. The latest study now establishes the importance of this mechanism in a larger group of patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

A Blood Test Could Lead to More Targeted IBD Treatments

Beyond explaining a previously mysterious cause of intestinal inflammation, the discovery could have important implications for patient care.

Researchers believe the results provide a foundation for developing a blood test that identifies people whose disease is associated with antibodies against IL-10. Such a test could help doctors recognize these patients earlier and select treatments that address the underlying immune malfunction.

Dr. Rainer Doffinger, a clinical immunologist at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, highlighted the potential benefits for both patients and healthcare systems.

"By identifying patients early and giving them targeted treatment, we could reduce reliance on expensive ongoing therapy and prevent complications. Even modest reductions in biologic treatment, admissions and surgery could translate into savings of many millions of pounds annually for the NHS, alongside the major benefits for patients through fewer interventions, improved quality of life or even durable remission."

Targeting the antibodies themselves, or the immune cells responsible for producing them, could offer a new treatment strategy for this particular group of patients. The approach could potentially reduce the need for repeated therapies, hospital admissions, and surgery while improving the chances of sustained disease control.

Professor Simon Travis, Professor of Clinical Gastroenterology at the University of Oxford and the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, emphasized the significance of identifying a specific biological cause of IBD.

"This is the most exciting discovery in a lifetime specialising in IBD. It means that we can now identify a group where we know what is causing the disease and that creates a real opportunity to change how we manage this disease."

The research marks an important advance toward personalized treatment for inflammatory bowel disease. Rather than relying primarily on symptoms to guide medical decisions, doctors may eventually be able to use biological testing to determine what is driving inflammation in individual patients and choose more appropriate therapies.

The study involved researchers from the Nuffield Department of Medicine at the University of Oxford, Newcastle University's Translational and Clinical Research Institute, and the Department of Immunology at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

Funding was provided through the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centres in Oxford, Cambridge, and Newcastle.

#5784. Gene Therapy Under Scrutiny After Nine Tumor Reports

— Novartis acknowledges reports in SMA patients treated with Zolgensma

Drugmaker Novartis acknowledged Thursday that there have been nine reports of tumors in children treated with its gene therapy onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).

Two of the tumor cases were linked to the drug, the company said.

Zolgensma, an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector-based gene therapy, was approved in 2019 to treat pediatric patients under 2 years of age with SMA and bi-allelic SMN1 mutations.

"Since first approval in 2019, Novartis has received 9 reports of tumors in patients previously treated with Zolgensma," a Novartis spokesperson wrote in an email to MedPage Today.

"Of those, two cases to date have shown evidence of vector DNA integration into the DNA of the patients. In both cases, the patients underwent treatment and continue to be monitored," the spokesperson continued. "In each case, we timely and appropriately notified health authorities and will continue to work with them on next steps."

The spokesperson did not say when tumors may have developed in the other seven cases, or when they were identified.

SMA is caused by reduced levels of the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein due to deletions or mutations in the SMN1 gene. A nearly identical gene, SMN2, produces low levels of functional SMN protein.

Onasemnogene abeparvovec uses an AAV vector to replace the SMN1 gene. Its prescribing information notes a theoretical risk of tumorigenicity from the integration of AAV vector DNA into the genome.

"The potential risk of tumors due to vector integration is currently included in the Zolgensma prescribing information," Novartis said.

Advocates recently raised concerns on social media after learning from their doctors that Novartis had received reports of tumors in patients treated with the gene therapy. SMA Europe, an umbrella organization of SMA patient groups in Europe, acknowledged the reports in a news release early Thursday.

"We understand that the relevant regulatory authorities are actively involved and are currently assessing the available evidence and determining what further steps may be needed," SMA Europe stated. "We trust in the regulatory processes established to evaluate safety signals and to take the necessary measures to protect patients and ensure the continued safety of medicines on the market."

In the U.S., the Muscular Dystrophy Association (MDA) said it was "seeking additional information, reviewing the available scientific and safety data with clinical and research experts, and has reached out to Novartis."

The MDA added that "limited information is available currently about the timing of events, nature of the tumors, and any future monitoring of treated individuals that may become appropriate."

A 2023 case report described a 16-month-old boy with SMA who was diagnosed with an epithelioid neoplasm of the spinal cord 14 months after receiving onasemnogene abeparvovec; the finding was considered inconclusive. A 2025 case report detailed a pilocytic astrocytoma in a child with SMA treated with onasemnogene abeparvovec; a molecular analysis suggested tumorigenesis was causally independent of the gene therapy.

Earlier this year, researchers identified vector integration in a brain tumor in a 5-year-old boy with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome) who received another AAV gene therapy, describing the case in the New England Journal of Medicine.

More than 6,000 patients have been treated with Zolgensma in clinical trials, managed access programs, and commercial treatment, Novartis said. "As part of Novartis' ongoing commitment to monitoring the safety of our medicines, we continually evaluate new safety information and assess all reported cases," the company added.

The tumor reports are not the first controversy involving Zolgensma. Soon after the therapy was approved, the FDA criticized the Novartis AveXis unit over data manipulation that affected the accuracy of animal product-testing results.

#5783. A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms

A cavity doesn't always have to mean drilling, injections, or an uncomfortable visit to the dentist. A major clinical trial has confirmed that a simple, inexpensive liquid can stop tooth decay in young children, potentially preventing painful infections and the need for dental surgery.

The treatment, called silver diamine fluoride (SDF), takes only seconds to apply to each affected tooth. Rather than removing damaged tooth material and placing a filling, a dentist uses a tiny sponge tipped applicator to paint the liquid directly onto the cavity. The process requires no drilling, injections, or sedation.

The findings could have enormous implications for childhood dental care. Every year, thousands of young children in the United States visit emergency departments because of untreated cavities. Emergency physicians generally cannot provide the dental procedures needed to address the underlying problem, leaving some children with ongoing pain and infections. Others ultimately need dental surgery under general anesthesia, which makes them completely unconscious during the procedure.

Now, researchers led by the University of Michigan have produced compelling evidence that a much simpler approach can stop many cavities from getting worse.

Major Clinical Trial Confirms Silver Diamine Fluoride Works

Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Phase III clinical trial included 830 children younger than 6. Participants were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa.

Head Start and Early Head Start are federally supported programs that provide early childhood education and related services to eligible families.

The results showed that a solution containing 38% silver diamine fluoride successfully stopped decay in more than half of the affected baby teeth when treatment was provided at six month intervals.

Dentists refer to this as arresting tooth decay, meaning the damaged area stops deteriorating. Unlike a traditional filling, the treatment does not replace lost tooth structure. Instead, it helps prevent existing decay from progressing.

SDF works through the combined effects of silver and fluoride. Silver helps combat bacteria associated with tooth decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the mineral structure of teeth and resist further damage.

"This is a very effective and safe treatment -- even in children as young as 1," said Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator.

A Simple Treatment Could Help Millions Avoid Dental Pain

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Although cavities may initially cause few noticeable symptoms, untreated decay can eventually lead to severe toothaches, infections, problems eating and sleeping, missed school days, and repeated medical appointments.

For young children, conventional dental treatment can also be particularly challenging. Some are too young to remain still throughout a procedure, while others experience significant fear or anxiety.

SDF offers an alternative for many of these patients because it can be applied quickly without the equipment and procedures required for a traditional filling.

Fontana said the benefits could extend well beyond young children. Older adults, people with developmental or physical disabilities, individuals with severe dental anxiety, and patients who have difficulty obtaining conventional dental care could also benefit.

There is, however, one important tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed portion of a treated tooth dark, which can be especially noticeable on front teeth. The discoloration is primarily cosmetic, but it may influence whether patients and families choose the treatment.

For many people, avoiding pain, drilling, or more invasive procedures may outweigh that drawback.

Why This Decades-Old Treatment Could Soon Reach More Patients

Silver diamine fluoride is not a newly invented substance. Dentists have successfully used it to manage cavities in numerous countries for decades.

In the United States, the FDA approved SDF as a medical device for treating tooth sensitivity in 2014. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities, meaning they apply an authorized product for a purpose beyond its original approved indication.

What has been missing is large-scale clinical evidence from U.S. populations establishing its safety and effectiveness for treating tooth decay, a key step toward obtaining FDA approval for that specific use.

The University of Michigan trial was designed to help fill that gap.

"If we want more children and families to benefit from this treatment, we need rigorous evidence showing both that it works and that it's safe. From a public health perspective, if we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in U.S. populations, and we now have that," Fontana said.

The investigation began in 2018 and continued despite the major disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The researchers believe stronger clinical evidence could make SDF more widely available, including in pediatric medical settings where children often receive care long before their first dental appointment.

"In medicine, clinicians want high-quality evidence before changing practice," Fontana said. "It is important to have data they can refer to because young children often see pediatricians years before they ever visit a dentist, broader acceptance could allow many more cavities to be treated while a referral to a dental home is successful, and before they become painful, infected or require surgery."

A dental home refers to an ongoing relationship with a dental care provider who can deliver preventive care, treatment, and follow-up services.

Expanding access to SDF could allow more children to receive early intervention before relatively manageable cavities develop into serious dental problems.

FDA Approval Could Expand Access to Cavity Treatment

The trial brought together researchers from the University of Michigan, New York University, the University of Iowa, and Indiana University. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, provided more than $12 million in funding.

The product tested was Advantage Arrest 38% SDF, supplied by Elevate Oral Care.

The findings provide clinical trial evidence that the manufacturer can use in an application seeking FDA approval of SDF as a drug for arresting dental caries, the medical term for tooth decay.

Amr Moursi, a professor of pediatric dentistry at New York University College of Dentistry and a co-principal investigator, emphasized the potential importance of that regulatory change.

"Our results support FDA approval of SDF for managing arrest of tooth decay in young children. Removing SDF from off-label status would be an important innovation which could lead to increased utilization by providers, enhanced payments by insurers and more consistent product quality," said Moursi, a co-principal investigator on the study.

For some children, receiving another application of SDF every few months could be sufficient to keep a cavity under control until the affected baby tooth naturally falls out.

Adults could also benefit, either by using SDF to manage decay over a longer period or as a temporary solution until a filling or another restorative procedure becomes affordable or practical.

The treatment is not suitable for every cavity, and stopping decay does not necessarily eliminate the need for future dental work. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that a procedure requiring only seconds to perform could help many patients avoid more complicated treatment.

"For almost anyone, this can arrest the decay and stop the infection and the pain it causes," Fontana said. "This could benefit many people."

Materials provided by University of Michigan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
